reader.summary: The week in Japan was dominated by the Bank of Japan holding interest rates while declaring its 2% inflation target finally reached after decades of deflation, with a hawkish tilt pointing toward further tightening in December. On security, Washington and Tokyo agreed to build a joint missile production facility in Japan, and Chancellor Merz visited to advance the GCAP fighter jet program, deepening defense cooperation. In a cultural-diplomatic flashpoint, Sanrio severed Hello Kitty's tie-up with a Japanese spy drama after China's public backlash. A surge in cyberattacks, including a GMO hack hitting forex brokers, prompted the prime minister to promise a swift response. In sports, Wales completed a dominant double over Japan in the WXV rugby series, while in tennis Rybakina secured her year-end number one ranking before withdrawing from Tokyo with an injury and Osaka was knocked out in the second round. Former PM Yasuo Fukuda and manga legend Tetsuya Chiba both died. The revised Imperial succession law reinforcing male-only heirs took effect amid a court challenge. Nidec announced it would sue its founder over Japan's biggest accounting fraud in a decade.

key_events.event: Bank of Japan held rates and declared the 2% inflation target reached, signaling a hawkish path toward further tightening in December.
The United States and Japan agreed to establish a joint missile production facility in Japan as US stockpiles dwindle.
Sanrio severed Hello Kitty's tie-up with a Japanese spy drama after China's public backlash, apologising and scrapping the partnership.
A surge in cyberattacks, including a GMO hack that hit forex brokers, prompted the prime minister to vow a prompt response and companies to compensate users.
Wales completed a dominant double over Japan in the WXV Global Series rugby, winning both matches including a 17-0 shutout in Tokyo.
Former Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, Japan's first second-generation PM and proponent of ties with China, died at 90.
Manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, creator of the boxing classic Ashita no Joe, died at 87.
Japan's revised Imperial succession law reinforcing male-only heirs took effect, with a cartoonist taking it to court.
Nidec announced it would sue its founder over his role in what is being called Japan's biggest accounting fraud in a decade.
A US Marine was indicted in Okinawa for the murder and robbery of a woman.

The Hello Kitty China spat (headlines 30, 61, 66, 75, 87), the FIFA/Infantino resignation (headlines 45, 54, 65, 86), and the Nidec fraud suit (headline 89) gave the week a strong drama-and-scandal flavour.

developments.subject: Hello Kitty and the China spat

developments.subject: Imperial succession law

developments.subject: Nidec accounting fraud

developments.subject: US Marine Okinawa indictment

developments.subject: Energy and fuel policy

display.eli5:
Japan's central bank just said inflation hit its 2 percent target and hinted at another rate hike in December. Next week, the yen will get stronger and bond prices will drop because everyone is betting the Bank of Japan will actually raise rates. Companies will start talking about how the days of nearly-free money are over.

On the security side, the United States and Japan agreed to build a missile factory in Japan, and Germany's chancellor came to talk about a shared fighter jet. Opposition parties in Japan will grumble about the cost and who controls the factory, and China will grumble about the whole thing getting closer to its borders.

A big hack hit a Japanese internet company and its forex customers, and the government promised a fast response. Next week it will actually announce what that response looks like: new money, a new task force, tighter rules for banks and brokers.

A surprise to watch: the Nidec accounting fraud case could blow up into a full boardroom fight, with the founder putting out a public statement and the board setting up a special investigation committee. That would turn a corporate lawsuit into a national conversation about how Japanese companies are run.

history_used.HISTORY_BULLETINS:
Round 2026-10-24:
Japan's news cycle was dominated by the historic launch of a spacecraft on a round-trip mission to Mars' moon Phobos, aiming to collect and return soil samples for the first time. On the economic front, core inflation surged to 2.1%, exceeding the Bank of Japan's target and cementing near-term rate-hike expectations, even as the BOJ signalled it might raise its inflation forecast while holding rates steady. Exports grew 16.7% in September on AI chip and auto demand, though one report framed the same figure as a 'huge miss' and a slowdown, and manufacturing PMI hit a seven-month low. PM Takaichi's approval rating slipped below 50% amid a cabinet scandal, and she publicly rejected criticism of the weak yen and high interest rates. Security saw the US ban BYD vehicles from a strategic air base, joint US-Japan drills around islands (partially disrupted by Typhoon Champi), and a Japanese journalist remaining jailed
- Mars moon Phobos mission (dominant, new): Japan launched a spacecraft on the first-ever round-trip mission to collect and return soil samples from Mars' moon Phobos, with French participation aboard.
- Inflation and BOJ rate policy (dominant, escalating): Core inflation hit 2.1%, exceeding the BOJ target, while the central bank signalled readiness to raise rates and may lift its inflation forecast at the upcoming policy meeting.
- Takaichi political troubles (regular, escalating): PM Takaichi's approval fell below 50% amid a cabinet scandal, and she pushed back on criticism of the weak yen and high interest rates as her one-year promises faced a reality check.
- US-Japan security and BYD ban (regular, continuing): The US banned BYD vehicles from a strategic air base in Japan over security concerns while the two countries kicked off joint drills around the islands.
- Japan-Russia journalist detention (regular, continuing): A Japanese journalist remained jailed in Moscow, described by analysts as the latest sign of eroding bilateral ties.
- Cyber threats and PHP flaws (regular, new): Japanese banks and airlines went offline patching critical PHP vulnerabilities, and a Chinese AI tool linked to Korean bank hacks was also used in Japan, prompting BOJ warnings.
- Trade, exports, and rare earths (regular, continuing): September exports grew 16.7% on chip and auto demand, but Japan faces a trade deficit from soaring oil imports, a manufacturing PMI at a seven-month low, and a rare-earth supply squeeze from China.
- Typhoon Champi (occasional, new): Typhoon Champi battered Taiwan and Japan, causing flight cancellations and disrupting US-Japan joint military drills.
- US-Myanmar talks in Tokyo (occasional, continuing): Japan's envoy Sasakawa met Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing, and the US held further secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo.
- Defense spending and fiscal policy (occasional, continuing): Finance Minister Katayama vowed fiscal prudence on defense funding while the government explored broadening the definition of security spending to inflate defense outlays.
- Sports: rugby and tennis (occasional, new): Fiji stunned Japan in a rugby match, Katie Boulter reached the Japan Open semi-final, and the Saudi Asian Cup was thrown into doubt by security concerns.
- Energy and power costs (occasional, continuing): Japan's power price hit a four-year high on rising coal and LNG costs, and the government weighed phasing out gasoline subsidies while considering re-introducing gas and electricity subsidies.

Round 2026-10-17:
Japan's week was defined by a diplomatic shock: Russia arrested and detained a Japanese journalist in its Far East region on suspicion of espionage, prompting Tokyo to formally demand explanations and rebuke Moscow. PM Takaichi publicly denied any spying allegations, and the incident became the latest flare-up in already strained Russia-Japan relations. On the economic front, Japan committed up to twenty-one billion dollars to finance two new GlobalFoundries semiconductor plants in New York, a major bet on reshoring advanced chip production and deepening US-Japan industrial ties. The International Monetary Fund also projected India would overtake Japan as the world's fourth-largest economy by 2027, a symbolic milestone that drew broad commentary. Domestically, Takaichi's cabinet suffered its first resignation when the farm minister stepped down amid a scandal; a replacement was quickly named. Takaichi's offhand remark that household chores and makeup add hours to her workday ignited a nationwide debate about gender
- Russia arrests Japanese journalist (dominant, new): Russia detained a Japanese reporter in its Far East on espionage suspicion, Tokyo formally rebuked Moscow, and Takaichi denied any spying allegations.
- GlobalFoundries chip deal (regular, new): Japan agreed to finance up to twenty-one billion dollars for two new GlobalFoundries semiconductor plants in New York.
- Farm minister resignation (regular, new): Japan's farm minister stepped down amid a scandal, the first exit from Takaichi's cabinet, and a new minister was appointed the same day.
- Takaichi gender-role debate (regular, new): Takaichi's remark that chores and makeup add hours to her workday triggered a public discussion about the expectations placed on a female prime minister.
- India overtakes Japan economically (regular, new): The IMF projected India would surpass Japan as the world's fourth-largest economy by 2027, a milestone that drew analyst commentary on Japan's relative standing.
